headline: IM Cannabis Q3 revenue falls 68% to C$1.65M after Germany exit
dek: IM Cannabis reported Q3 revenue of C$1.65 million and a C$7.08 million net loss on 13 November, as cash limits cut imports and a drone deal is negotiated.
key_points: IM Cannabis said third-quarter revenue was C$1.65 million, down 68% from C$5.08 million a year earlier, with a gross loss of C$35,000.
Total net loss widened to C$7.08 million from C$3.87 million; nine-month revenue fell 43% to C$8.96 million.

The company blamed lower Israeli sales and reduced imports driven partly by cash-flow constraints, and ended September with C$2.42 million in cash and restricted cash against a C$5.50 million working-capital deficit.
It sold its European business, including German distributor Adjupharm, on 29 September and is negotiating a 51% stake in a Polish drone company.
body: IM Cannabis, the Nasdaq-listed medical cannabis company that now operates only in Israel, reported a steep fall in sales for the third quarter. Revenue for the three months to 30 September was C$1.65 million, against C$5.08 million a year earlier, the company said in results released after the market closed on 13 November. It booked a gross loss of C$35,000 and a total net loss of C$7.08 million, compared with a net loss of C$3.87 million in the same quarter of 2025.

The results are the first since IM Cannabis sold its European operations in September, and they show a business shrinking fast while management negotiates a move into a very different industry: military drones in Poland.

On a continuing-operations basis, the management's discussion and analysis filed with the SEC shows revenue down 68% in the quarter and 43% over nine months, to C$8.96 million from C$15.77 million. Gross margin, which the company calculates before fair-value adjustments, swung from 31% a year earlier to minus 2%. Operating loss rose to C$3.04 million from C$1.92 million, and the loss from continuing operations reached C$4.67 million, against C$1.40 million a year before.

Adjusted EBITDA, a non-IFRS measure, was a loss of C$2.63 million in the quarter. For the nine months, total net loss including discontinued operations came to C$13.93 million, compared with C$3.88 million in the first nine months of 2025.

The quarterly summary in the filing puts the drop in context. It lists revenue of C$8.68 million for the first quarter of 2026 and C$7.59 million for the second, before the C$1.65 million third quarter. Only the third-quarter figure is marked as continuing operations, so the earlier quarters may include the European business that has since been sold. Even allowing for that, the step down is large: third-quarter revenue was less than a quarter of the second quarter's reported figure.
> A medical cannabis importer that cannot afford to import is no longer really a cannabis business, whatever the filing calls it.

The company gave a plain reason. Lower revenue in Israel reflected changes in product mix, pricing and volume, it said, as well as reduced imports driven in part by cash-flow constraints, which cut the amount it could sell. Cost of revenue fell 30% over nine months, but not as fast as sales, which is why gross profit turned negative in the quarter.

The balance sheet explains the cash problem. At 30 September, IM Cannabis held C$2.42 million in cash and restricted cash and had a working-capital deficit of C$5.50 million, meaning current liabilities exceeded current assets by that amount. Operating activities used C$1.59 million of cash in the first nine months. The company said its stated goal for 2026 remains profitability, supported by new supply-chain processes and a better supplier base.

On 29 September the company completed the sale of its European-focused operations, including its German subsidiary Adjupharm GmbH, to Slil.com Holding. The price included a C$3 million advance payment and the buyer's assumption of certain liabilities of up to C$9.4 million. IM Cannabis expects the deal to lift shareholders' equity by about C$3 million. It kept its Israeli medical cannabis business, which imports and distributes cannabis to patients and runs retail pharmacies and online platforms.

The exit takes IM Cannabis out of Germany, Europe's largest medical cannabis market, at a time when the market is under price pressure. Industry data presented in Germany this month showed flower prices falling and thousands of products competing for pharmacy shelf space, as we reported on 9 November.
## A drone deal on the table

The biggest change may be still to come. In September the company signed a non-binding agreement to buy 51% of Space Defense Innovations, a Polish company in the unmanned aerial systems sector. Its subsidiary, BlueAero Group, distributes tactical drone products made by BlueBird Aero Systems. IM Cannabis said it is negotiating a definitive share purchase agreement with the Polish company's shareholders. The agreement is not binding, and the company has not disclosed a price.
IM Cannabis is listed on Nasdaq under the ticker IMCC. The third-quarter loss per share from continuing operations was C$6.65, according to the filing.

The first signal is whether IM Cannabis signs a binding deal for the Polish drone business, and on what terms, given its thin cash position. The second is fourth-quarter revenue: if imports stay constrained, sales in Israel could fall again. Investors will also watch for new financing, since a working-capital deficit of C$5.50 million against C$2.42 million in cash leaves little room. The company's full interim financial statements and MD&A are available on SEDAR+ and EDGAR.
